subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a geographical enquiry, what is a hypothesis?
options: A testable statement or prediction that the fieldwork sets out to investigate
A summary of the results collected in the field
A list of all the equipment needed for fieldwork
A map showing the location of the study area
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a predictive statement, often written so it can be supported or rejected by the data collected.

questions.q: Which of these is normally the FIRST stage of the fieldwork enquiry process?
options: Identifying an aim or hypothesis to investigate
Presenting the data as graphs
Writing the conclusion
Collecting data in the field
questions.explain: The enquiry begins by setting an aim or hypothesis before any data is planned or collected.

questions.q: Why is a hypothesis usually written as a clear statement rather than an open question?
options: So that the collected data can be used to support or reject it
Because questions are not allowed in coursework
So that no data collection is needed
Because it makes the fieldwork take longer
questions.explain: A statement hypothesis gives a definite prediction that the evidence can directly test.

questions.q: A student writes: 'This report will investigate how land use changes with distance from the CBD.' This sentence is best described as the enquiry's...
options: Aim
Conclusion
Method of sampling
Data presentation technique
questions.explain: The aim states the overall purpose of the enquiry, guiding what data is collected.

questions.q: What is primary data?
options: Data collected first-hand by the student during fieldwork
Data taken from a published textbook
Data downloaded from a national census website
Data borrowed from another student's old project
questions.explain: Primary data is original information gathered directly by the investigator in the field.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of secondary data?
options: Population figures from a national census
A pedestrian count carried out by the student
Field sketches drawn on site
Measurements of river width taken with a tape measure
questions.explain: Secondary data is obtained from existing published sources rather than collected first-hand.

questions.q: What is the key difference between quantitative and qualitative data?
options: Quantitative data is numerical, whereas qualitative data describes qualities or opinions
Quantitative data is always secondary, whereas qualitative data is always primary
Qualitative data is numerical, whereas quantitative data is descriptive
There is no difference between the two
questions.explain: Quantitative data can be counted or measured, while qualitative data records descriptions, views or impressions.

questions.q: In systematic sampling, how are the sampling points chosen?
options: At regular, fixed intervals, such as every 10 metres
Completely at random using random numbers
By dividing the population into groups first
By selecting only the most interesting sites
questions.explain: Systematic sampling selects points at a set interval to give even coverage of the area.

questions.q: Which sampling method uses chance so that every point has an equal opportunity of being selected?
options: Random sampling
Systematic sampling
Stratified sampling
Quota sampling
questions.explain: Random sampling relies on chance, for example using random number tables or grid references, so bias is reduced.

questions.q: A town has 70% adults and 30% teenagers. A student surveys 70 adults and 30 teenagers to match these proportions. Which sampling method is this?
options: Stratified sampling
Random sampling
Systematic sampling
Point sampling
questions.explain: Stratified sampling divides a population into groups and samples each in proportion to its size.

questions.q: A questionnaire given to shoppers is an example of collecting which type of primary data?
options: Human/social data through people's responses
Physical data about river discharge
Secondary data from official records
Geological data about rock type
questions.explain: Questionnaires gather human data by recording the views and characteristics of people.

questions.q: To test the hypothesis 'The CBD is the busiest part of the town', which primary method is most suitable?
options: Carrying out pedestrian counts at sites across the town
Reading the town's population total from a census
Drawing an annotated field sketch of one building
Measuring the width of the local river
questions.explain: Pedestrian counts provide comparable numerical data on how busy each location is.

questions.q: In a river study, which equipment would you use to measure the width of the channel?
options: A tape measure stretched across the channel
A float and a stopwatch
An anemometer
A clinometer only
questions.explain: Channel width is measured directly by stretching a tape measure from one bank to the other.

questions.q: When measuring river velocity, why might a student time a float over a set distance several times and take an average?
options: To reduce the effect of anomalies and improve reliability
To make the river flow faster
Because one reading is not allowed in fieldwork
To change the width of the river
questions.explain: Repeating measurements and averaging reduces the impact of one unusual reading, improving reliability.

questions.q: Which graph is most suitable for showing the relationship between two variables, such as river depth and velocity?
options: A scatter graph
A pie chart
A single bar
A located proportional symbol only
questions.explain: A scatter graph plots paired values and shows whether two variables are correlated.

questions.q: A pie chart is the most appropriate way to present which kind of data?
options: Proportions of a whole, such as percentage land use in an area
Change in temperature over time
The relationship between depth and velocity
The exact grid reference of a site
questions.explain: Pie charts show how a total is divided into parts, ideal for percentages of a whole.

questions.q: A student has measured river width at ten sites moving downstream and wants to show how it changes with distance. Which presentation is most appropriate?
options: A line graph of width against distance downstream
A pie chart of the ten values
A single bar for the largest site
A questionnaire summary table
questions.explain: A line graph clearly shows a continuous trend or change over distance.

questions.q: In the analysis stage of an enquiry, what does a student mainly do?
options: Describe and explain the patterns and trends shown by the data
Decide on the hypothesis to test
Collect the primary data in the field
Choose the equipment for measurements
questions.explain: Analysis involves interpreting the presented data, describing patterns and giving geographical reasons for them.

questions.q: What is an anomaly in a set of fieldwork results?
options: A reading that does not fit the general pattern of the data
The average of all the readings
The title given to a graph
The most common result in the data
questions.explain: An anomaly is an unexpected value that differs from the overall trend and should be identified in analysis.

questions.q: What should a conclusion in a fieldwork enquiry mainly do?
options: State whether the evidence supports or rejects the hypothesis
List all the equipment used
Introduce a brand new hypothesis to test
Describe how to draw a bar chart
questions.explain: The conclusion returns to the original hypothesis and judges whether the data supports it.

questions.q: In the evaluation stage, a student mainly considers...
options: The limitations and reliability of the methods and how the study could be improved
Which snacks to bring on the fieldtrip
The colour of the graphs used
How to write the hypothesis
questions.explain: Evaluation critically reflects on problems, accuracy and reliability, and suggests improvements.

questions.q: A student collected data at only one site on one afternoon. Which evaluation point is most valid?
options: The small, one-off sample may not be representative, reducing reliability
The data must be perfectly reliable because it was primary
No improvements are possible for this study
The hypothesis cannot be written afterwards
questions.explain: A limited sample taken once may not reflect wider or long-term patterns, weakening reliability.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Geography (0460) syllabus; Coursework / Alternative to Coursework (Fieldwork)
